title: Evolving Pydantic: `BaseStruct`
body:
This is a feature plan for the next step in the `pydantic` API, which we'd like to call `BaseStruct`.

The high-level goal is to take some of the lessons we've learned from `BaseModel`, and present a new type which should achieve higher performance, more features and better default semantics. `BaseModel` may eventually gain some of these changes itself, but we would prefer to be extremely conservative with changing `BaseModel` and introduce a new type so that users can opt-in to the changed semantics.

We will merge `BaseStruct` into the `pydantic.experimental.structs` namespace while this type is being developed, possibly as soon as Pydantic 2.13. We anticipate that Pydantic V3 may be the milestone where `BaseStruct` is stabilised, although this is not strictly required.

Rough outline of the planned semantics of `BaseStruct`:

- Performance
   - [ ] `BaseStruct` is planned to keep more data as (internal?) native state rather than Python objects
   - [ ] Field accessors will probably be cached so that once the Python value is accessed, it will have normal Python semantics
- Ergonomics
   - [ ] `BaseStruct` will have no methods (`model_validate`, `model_dump`). Instead we will expose free functions such as `validate`, `validate_json`, `to_python` and `to_json`
   - [ ] There will likely be a `StructMethodsMixin` type to add methods such as `struct_validate` where desired
   - [ ] We might try to do something different with generic structs so that we don't create new subclasses when doing generic parameterisation, and just make "regular" generic aliases.
- Features
  - [ ] We would like to eventually offer compatibilty between struct types and dataframes, particularly arrow "struct arrays". The exact form of this is yet to be explored.

title: Allow a custom error message when a regex pattern isn't matched for a Field
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

In our code we have several places where we have code like the following in order to provide both a nice error message at runtime and a JSON schema compatible regex:

```
DEBIAN_PACKAGE_NAME_REGEX = r"^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.+-]+$"


def _validate_debian_package_name(name: str) -> str:
    """Validate a Debian package name."""
    if not re.match(DEBIAN_PACKAGE_NAME_REGEX, name):
        raise ValueError("Nice error message goes here")
    return name


DebianPackageName = Annotated[
    str,
    pydantic.Field(pattern=DEBIAN_PACKAGE_NAME_REGEX),
    pydantic.BeforeValidator(_validate_debian_package_name),
]
```

This works fine, but is a bit redundant. It would be nice to have an optional parameter for `Field` that replaces the "string should match pattern" message with a custom error message.

body: I was working on a kind of abstraction idea, where you define a certain kind of API as a `dataclass` structure with generics, where the general abstraction is shared between services and every service may narrow the generics with its own implementation... ```python @dataclass class Foo: bar: str = "baz" @dataclass class API[FOO]: foo: FOO # define your concret API @dataclass class MyFoo: extra: int = 123 @dataclass class MyAPI[FOO](API[FOO]): ... api_data = TypeAdapter(API).dump_json(API(foo=Foo("xyz"))) api = TypeAdapter(MyAPI[MyFoo]).validate_json(api_data) ``` The issue is, that basically deserializing into `API[MyFoo]` works as expected, but `MyAPI[MyFoo]` not. I put together a `pytest`, which highlights all generic circumstances (with flipped assertions, so that it succeeds within the actual implementation of pydantic): Python: 3.14.2 pydantic: 2.12.5 ```python from dataclasses import dataclass as dataclass_std import pytest from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass as dataclass_pydantic # title: No psycopg_async scheme in PostgresDsn network class
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

SQLAlchemy has two dialects of psycopg: psycopg2 (psycopg package version version 2) and psycopg (psycopg version 3)
The asyncio version of the dialect psycopg (version 3) may also be specified explicitly using the psycopg_async suffix, as:

```
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

asyncio_engine = create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+psycopg_async://scott:tiger@localhost/test"
)
```
https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/dialects/postgresql.html#module-sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql.psycopg

But pydantic settings field with type PostgresDSN do not allow this suffix in schemes. Because "postgresql+psycopg_async" not in allowed schemes in PostgresDSN class.
https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/pydantic/networks.py#L755



### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import PostgresDsn
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class PostgresSettings(BaseSettings):
    DSN: PostgresDsn | None = "postgresql+psycopg_async://user:password@postgres:5432/postgres"
```

title: deep-copying `MISSING` crashes in `BaseModel.model_construct()` and `BaseModel.__deepcopy__()` (TypeError: Cannot pickle 'Sentinel' object)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

## Problem
When a field’s default is the experimental `MISSING` sentinel (pydantic >=2.12), Pydantic ends up trying to deepcopy that sentinel in a few places. The sentinel isn’t deepcopy/pickle-friendly, so this raises: 

> TypeError: Cannot pickle 'Sentinel' object.

## Where it happens
- `BaseModel.model_construct()`: default resolution goes through `smart_deepcopy()`, which currently tries to deepcopy `MISSING`.
- `BaseModel.__deepcopy__()`: stdlib `deepcopy()` is called on `self.__dict__` (and others), which hits `MISSING` and fails.

## Proposed fix
1) In `smart_deepcopy()`, return early for the sentinel:

```python
# pydantic/_internal/_utils.py
from pydantic_core import MISSING

def smart_deepcopy(obj):
    if obj is MISSING:
        return obj
    # rest of current logic...
```

This keeps the singleton by identity and avoids deepcopy entirely.

2) In `BaseModel.__deepcopy__()`, use `smart_deepcopy()` (with memo) instead of raw `deepcopy()` for model internals.

- Today it does `deepcopy(self.__dict__, memo=...)`; that will crash if values contain `MISSING`.
- `smart_deepcopy()` doesn’t accept memo yet, it could be extended to do so and thread it into the fallback deepcopy call.

## Rationale
- `MISSING` is a singleton sentinel meant to be passed by identity. Copying it isn’t useful and currently fails.
- Using `smart_deepcopy()` in `BaseModel.__deepcopy__()` aligns behavior between construction and copying and avoids duplicating special cases.

## Minimal repro
```python
from copy import deepcopy
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from pydantic.experimental.missing_sentinel import MISSING  # 2.12.x

class M(BaseModel):
    a: int | MISSING = Field(default=MISSING)

# 1) model_construct path
M.model_construct()  # attempts to deepcopy MISSING -> TypeError

# 2) __deepcopy__ path
m = M()
deepcopy(m)          # deepcopy(self.__dict__) hits MISSING -> TypeError
```

Expected

title: Preserve `NamedTuple` class during validation
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

This is what I'm observing:

```Python
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B


c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)

# expected: a_or_b=B(x=1)
# prints: a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

This short-circuits on type arguments in the union in order in the `smart` mode of unions (`left_to_right` I assume makes no difference, the problem lies in exactness).
If we reverse it, the output will show `B` because `B` was first that structurally matched.

It works this way in strict mode too.
This resembles `left_to_right` more than `smart` mode of the union schema.

Conceptually, Pydantic looks for ways to match namedtuple as a structural type, whereas the nominal bit was missed.

This applies to old-fashion named tuples as well:
```py
from collections import namedtuple

import pydantic

A = namedtuple('A', 'x')
B = namedtuple('B', 'x')

class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B

c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)  # a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

We would want to convert between uniform namedtuples in non-strict mode -- sure:

```py
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    only_a: A


c = C(only_a=B(x=1))
print(c)  # only_a=A(x=1)
```

but I'm not so sure we want the union schema to miss the nominal type of the input. If we can preserve the original type, my instinct is that we'd want to keep it. Esp. since we don't observe this behavior with dataclasses (namedtuples are of quite different nature, though).

The current behavior can be interpreted as a feature, not a bug -- feel free to relabel this as a feature request if you do think that's true.

## In short

I'm proposing a feature to, in validation, validate every namedtuple input against its targeted namedtuple class (so, `return_schema` -- seems like `return_schema` isn't used by namedtuple schemas yet) **before** proceeding with the call validator logic and deconstructing it as a collection of arguments and trying a call to the namedtuple constructor. It would be based on a new `idempotent` flag in `CallValidator` -- if a function call is idempotent, the validation should start from the return validator -- if that doesn't pass, only then try to call. As a result, nominal types wouldn't be swapped in unions of namedtuples in smart union mode.

Do you guys think this is worth adding to pydantic, or too much hassle for an edge case?
Thanks!

PS One more thing. This relies on the assumption that instance checks guarantees type safety of the object's state.

If the namedtuple instance contains unsound data, its internals wouldn't be re-validated and fixed up in place as it happens right now. In this sense, the change could be breaking. 

The same that would happen here already happens for dataclasses in Pydantic:

```py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import BaseModel


@dataclass
class Foo:
    x: int


malformed = Foo(x="1")

class Model(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo

print(Model(foo=malformed))
```

If someone has an unsure instance of a namedtuple, they would need to re-validate it through type adapter, perhaps.
Or just use models directly on raw data -- for 99.999% of people this won't happen.

title: repr when fields are aliased is misleading
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In Python, the [`repr`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#repr) of an object is most typically `eval`-able to reproduce the object. In the cases where that's not possible the usual convention is to surround the information with angle brackets rather than making it look like Python code.

pydantic's field aliases appear to break from this convention in ways that can easily pass unnoticed:

``` python
In [1]: import pydantic
   ...: 
   ...: class Foo(pydantic.BaseModel):
   ...:     aliased: int = pydantic.Field(42, alias="the_alias")
   ...: 

In [2]: Foo(the_alias=2)
Out[2]: Foo(aliased=2)  # huh, ok, I guess I can use that spelling too

In [3]: Foo(aliased=2)
Out[3]: Foo(aliased=42)  # doesn't match _and_ no error
```

I realise that if the field default is removed then an error is surfaced, however the error complains about a missing field rather than an extra/misspelled one. Additionally, field defaults are hardly uncommon.

I discovered this after attempting to use the non-aliased spelling which my type checker (`mypy`) encouraged me to use[^1], then finding that that didn't work as I expected it would. I haven't been able to find anything in the documentation to indicate that this is intentional.

[^1]: to me using the field names in `__init__` also feels more natural, even when there is an alias, since that's how e.g: dataclasses work

```python
    if flag:
```

body:
## Summary

In Click 8.2.0, completion for commands in nested groups doesn't work as expected anymore. Instead of completing command options and/or arguments, completion infinitely repeats the command names for the group.

## Example program

Inspired by the example in #2847 

Save the following as `bin/nested` in a virtualenv

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

# nested

import click


def _complete_arg(ctx, _, incomplete):
    values = [
        "foo",
        "bar",
        "foobar",
        "baz",
    ]
    return [v for v in values if v.startswith(incomplete)]

@click.group
def main():
    ...

@main.group
def subgroup():
    ...

@subgroup.command
@click.option("--name", help="Name of something.")
@click.argument("arg", shell_complete=_complete_arg)
def compile(name: str | None, arg: str) -> None:
    """Test argument completion in nested groups."""
    click.echo(f"{name=} {arg=}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main.main()
```

Run `eval "$(_NESTED_COMPLETE=bash_source nested)"` to setup completion (for bash)

## Completion behavior

|Prefix|8.2.0 completion suggestions (unexpected behavior)|8.1.8 completion suggestions (expected behavior)|
|-|-|-|
|`nested`|`subgroup`|`subgroup`|
|`nested subgroup`|`compile`|`compile`|
|`nested subgroup compile`|`compile`|`foo     bar     foobar  baz`|
|`nested subgroup compile f`|none|`foo     foobar`|
|`nested subgroup compile --`|`--help`|`--name  --help`|
|`nested subgroup compile --name=n`|`compile`|`foo     bar     foobar  baz`|

## Environment

- Python version: Python 3.12.3
- Click version: 8.2.0

## Initial debugging

Reverting 0ef55fda47bb3d0dece21197d81d8d72a4250e73 for `src/click/shell_completion.py` restores the 8.1.8 completion behavior.

Looking at the change, I believe that the bug is actually caused by a simple statement reordering . IMO https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/af73ce4793bf38edf11a16e959ef0d8a0dbf6c1f/src/click/shell_completion.py#L567-L571 should be the following to preserve the 8.1.8 behavior:

```python
                    with cmd.make_context(
                        name, args, parent=ctx, resilient_parsing=True
                    ) as sub_ctx:
                        ctx = sub_ctx
                        args = ctx._protected_args + ctx.args
```

Note that Click 8.1.8 directly assigns `cmd.make_context()` to `ctx` in the equivalent snippet: https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/934813e4d421071a1b3db3973c02fe2721359a6e/src/click/shell_completion.py#L530-L531

In the same fashion, I believe that lines 589 and 590 should be switched in https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/af73ce4793bf38edf11a16e959ef0d8a0dbf6c1f/src/click/shell_completion.py#L581-L590

title: `locals()` usage causes failures when debugging due to namespace pollution
body:
While debugging a call inside the library, I discovered that the code constructing request parameters is using `locals()`. This breaks when stepping through the function in a debugger.

The relevant code:

```python
all_args = locals()
all_args.pop("self")
all_args["model_id"] = all_args.pop("model")
kwargs = all_args.pop("kwargs")

if tools:
    all_args["tools"] = prepare_tools(tools, built_in_tools=self.BUILT_IN_TOOLS)

for i, message in enumerate(messages):
    if isinstance(message, ChatCompletionMessage):
        messages[i] = message.model_dump(
            exclude_none=True,
            exclude={"reasoning"},
        )
all_args["messages"] = messages

return await self._acompletion(CompletionParams(**all_args), **kwargs)
```

This works normally when executed without debugging. However, when stepping through the function in a debugger, the `CompletionParams` validation fails because `all_args` unexpectedly contains additional entries. Debuggers inject temporary variables into the local namespace for watch expressions, etc. When `locals()` is called during a debugging session, it captures these extra variables, which then get passed to `CompletionParams(**all_args)`, causing a validation error.

I've reproduced this with both VSCode's debugger and `pdb`. This is expected debugger behavior, not a debugger bug, `locals()` returns the current local namespace, which debuggers necessarily modify to function.

### Describe the bug

`tool_choice` is incorrectly translated from OpenAI's spec to Anthropic's spec.

### Example w/ Code

The following shows a correctly formatted request using `tools` and `tool_choice` with OpenAI's spec:
```python
from any_llm import completion

response = completion(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Extract the following: Hey I'm Bilel and I'm 28yo"}],
    tool_choice={"type": "function", "function": {"name": "User"}},
    tools=[
        {
            "type": "function",
            "function": {
                "name": "User",
                "description": "Correctly extracted `User` with all the required parameters with correct types",
                "parameters": {
                    "properties": {
                        "name": {"title": "Name", "type": "string"},
                        "age": {"title": "Age", "type": "integer"},
                    },
                    "required": ["age", "name"],
                    "type": "object",
                },
            },
        }
    ],
)
```

This runs correctly. Now, when switching to a Claude model:
```python
from any_llm import completion

response = completion(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Extract the following: Hey I'm Bilel and I'm 28yo"}],
    tool_choice={"type": "function", "function": {"name": "User"}},
    tools=[
        {
            "type": "function",
            "function": {
                "name": "User",
                "description": "Correctly extracted `User` with all the required parameters with correct types",
                "parameters": {
                    "properties": {
                        "name": {"title": "Name", "type": "string"},
                        "age": {"title": "Age", "type": "integer"},
                    },
                    "required": ["age", "name"],
                    "type": "object",
                },
            },
        }
    ],
)
```

The above code raises the following exception:
```
anthropic.BadRequestError: Error code: 400 - {'type': 'error', 'error': {'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'message': "tool_choice: Input tag '{'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': 'User'}}' found using 'type' does not match any of the expected tags: 'auto', 'any', 'tool', 'none'"}, 'request_id': 'req_011CVhEmofiCTqoYuhvREPMH'}
```

The `_convert_tool_choice` function incorrectly translates the `tool_choice` into `{'type': {'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': 'User'}}, 'disable_parallel_tool_use': False}`. This is incorrect syntax as per [Claude's API documentation on forcing tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use#forcing-tool-use). It should be `{"type": "tool", "name": "User"}`.

title: Use pytest-xdist to run some tests in parallel
body:
Thanks, Claude for the info

If you want to run your tests in parallel with pytest, especially when using parameterized tests (like with different `agent_framework` values), you can use the `pytest-xdist` plugin, which enables parallel test execution.

### How to Enable Parallel Test Execution

1. **Install pytest-xdist** (if you haven’t already):
   ```bash
   pip install pytest-xdist
   ```

2. **Run your tests with the `-n` flag** to specify the number of parallel workers:
   ```bash
   pytest -n auto
   ```
   or
   ```bash
   pytest -n 4
   ```
   (`auto` will use the number of CPU cores.)

3. **Marking tests as parallel-safe:**  
   By default, pytest-xdist will run all tests in parallel unless you use fixtures with `scope="session"` or other resources that aren’t thread/process safe.  
   You don’t need to add a special marker to each test to allow parallelism—pytest-xdist will handle it for you.

4. **If you want to explicitly mark a test as safe for parallel execution** (for documentation or future maintainers), you can use a custom marker, but this is not required for pytest-xdist to work. For example:
   ```python
   import pytest

   @pytest.mark.parallel
   def test_something():
       ...
   ```
   And then you could filter or select these tests, but again, this is just for your own organization.

### Special Note for Parametrized Tests
If you use `@pytest.mark.parametrize("agent_framework", [...])`, pytest-xdist will automatically distribute the different parameter combinations across workers.

### TL;DR
- Just install `pytest-xdist` and run with `-n auto` or `-n <num>`.
- No need to mark tests as parallel unless you want to for your own clarity.
- Make sure your tests don’t write to the same files or share mutable state!

---

If you want to ensure your test is safe for parallel execution, make sure:
- Each test uses its own temp files/directories (which you already do with `tmp_path`).
- No global state is mutated.

title: [DOC BUG] `rich.progress.track()` documentation uses "sequence" instead of "iterable"
body:
https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/progress.html#rich.progress.track reads:

> Parameters:
> sequence (Iterable[ProgressType]) – A sequence (must support “len”) you wish to iterate over.

In fact, the `sequence` parameter is not a sequence, it is an iterable (which is correctly detected by a documentation builder, btw), so it doesn't have to support `len`.

My suggestions:

* ~~add a parameter named `iterable` with the same meaning as `sequence`~~,
* ~~of course, keep `sequence` for backward compatibility~~,
(edit: I do agree with current solution. Thank you.)
* maybe change the type in the source code from `Sequence | Iterable` to just `Iterable`.

Sample program to play with (as you see, `concurrent.futures.as_completed()` is not a sequence—it is a generator—so it does not have `len`, and despite of that the code works correctly):

```python
#! /usr/bin/env --split-string=uv run --script

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.13"
# dependencies = [
#   "rich",
# ]
# ///

import concurrent.futures
import random
import time

import rich.progress
import rich.traceback


def main() -> None:
    """Top-level logic."""
    rich.traceback.install(show_locals=True)

    with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:

        futures = { executor.submit(simulate_job) for i in range(15) }

        for future in rich.progress.track(
                concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures),
                description='Working…',
                # total=len(futures),
                ):
            print('Something is done!')
        

def simulate_job() -> None:
    """Job simulator — sleep for a random amount of time."""
    time.sleep(
        random.uniform(0.1, 1.3),
        )
        

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

```python
logging.addHandler( RichHandler( console=Console( expand_tabs=False, file=sys.stderr ) ) )
```

for instance, I like log output to be valid TSV (TAB-Separated Values) files as well as prettily-rendered console output. This allows me to process large log files efficiently. Unfortunately, this isn't valid Rich. Since TAB _is_ a valid character to print to console, I consider not being able to do so a bug, rather than a feature request, as it is not currently possible for me to print the characters I want to console (TABs are getting replaced with space characters in RichHandler).
